questions.question: Explain the push and pull factors that drew black workers to the Kimberley diamond fields.
questions.expected_answer: Pull factors: wages higher than anything available in rural areas, and goods that could be bought, especially guns, which were sold freely in the early 1870s, as well as ploughs, blankets, clothing and cattle; some chiefs, such as Sekhukhune of the Pedi, sent young men to earn money for guns. Push factors: hut taxes payable in cash, loss of land to settlers so families could not live by farming alone, droughts, cattle diseases and wars, and the need for cattle for lobola. At first workers came by choice and had bargaining power, choosing employers and leaving when they wished; over time, taxes and land loss increasingly forced them into wage labour.

questions.question: What were pass laws and masters and servants laws, and how did they control black workers?
questions.expected_answer: From 1872 in Griqualand West, every black worker had to register, carry a pass showing name, employer and wage, and enter a contract; a worker without a pass could be arrested, fined, jailed or forced to work, and could leave only when the employer signed the pass. Masters and servants laws made breaking a contract, desertion or disobedience a criminal offence for workers, while employers faced at most civil claims. These laws stopped desertion, reduced competition between employers so wages stayed low, helped identify suspected diamond thieves and limited workers' freedom of movement. The system became a model for the Witwatersrand and for later national pass laws.

questions.question: Describe the closed compound system, the reasons the companies gave for it and its effects on black workers.
questions.expected_answer: From 1885, black workers lived in barracks around a yard, enclosed by high walls or fences with wire mesh, for their whole contract, usually three to six months, going to the mine through tunnels or guarded passages, searched daily and detained and searched again at the end of the contract. Companies said compounds stopped diamond theft and illicit diamond buying, stopped drinking, and kept workers at work for the whole contract. Effects: loss of freedom of movement and family life, prices set by company stores so part of wages returned to the company, overcrowding and disease with high death rates, and no ability to bargain. White workers were largely exempted after the 1884 strike, showing the racial division of labour. The system shaped later migrant labour on the gold mines.
